claim: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are aggressive sarcomas that typically carry a dismal prognosis.
source: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are aggressive sarcomas that typically carry a dismal prognosis.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement about MPNSTs supported by established medical knowledge in the field.

claim: MPNSTs are insensitive to traditional chemotherapy.
source: Given the insensitivity of these tumors to traditional chemotherapy and the absence of effective targeted drugs, new therapeutic strategies are urgently needed.
evidence: This statement draws from established clinical knowledge about MPNST treatment resistance.

claim: There are no effective targeted drugs for MPNSTs.
source: Given the insensitivity of these tumors to traditional chemotherapy and the absence of effective targeted drugs, new therapeutic strategies are urgently needed.
evidence: This statement reflects current clinical knowledge about the lack of approved targeted therapies.

claim: Photothermal therapy (PTT) at the third near-infrared biowindow (NIR-III) has demonstrated significant potential in cancer theranostics.
source: Photothermal therapy (PTT) including near-infrared laser at the third biowindow (NIR-III) has demonstrated significant potential in cancer theranostics due to its minimally invasive nature and excellent therapeutic outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on NIR-III applications.

claim: Poor target specificity and biocompatibility of photothermal agents (PTAs) hinder clinical translation of PTT.
source: However, the passive utilization of photothermal agents (PTAs) with poor target specificity and biocompatibility substantially hinders the clinical translation and application of this method.
evidence: This is based on known limitations of PTAs discussed in the literature.

claim: MPNSTs affect approximately 10% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
source: MPNSTs, which affect approximately 10% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and cause severe organ damage, are associated with high morbidity (Mowery and Clayburgh, 2019; Widemann, 2009).
evidence: This statistic is supported by citations to Mowery and Clayburgh, 2019 and Widemann, 2009.

claim: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy provide only limited benefits to MPNST patients.
source: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy provide only limited benefits to MPNST patients, and there is no targeted therapy approved for clinical use (Vitolo et al., 2019; van Noesel et al., 2019; Kroep et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vitolo et al., 2019; van Noesel et al., 2019; and Kroep et al., 2011.

claim: Extended resection with negative surgical margins is key to improving the prognosis of MPNST patients.
source: The key to improving the prognosis of MPNST patients is extended resection with negative surgical margins, which still faces problems such as the difficulty of surgery, high risk of local recurrence, and distant metastasis (Widemann and Italiano, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Widemann and Italiano, 2018.

claim: Inorganic PTAs have intrinsic issues such as poor biodegradability, disappointing processability, and apparent cytotoxicity.
source: However, inorganic PTAs have intrinsic issues such as poor biodegradability, disappointing processability, and apparent cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about limitations of inorganic materials.

claim: Optimization of photothermal conversion efficiency and photothermal stability is highly challenging for organic PTAs.
source: Although the advantageous properties of organic agents include distinct biodegradability and biocompatibility, optimization of photothermal conversion efficiency and photothermal stability is highly challenging (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: NIR light can be divided into four distinct regions: NIR-I (700–950 nm), NIR-II (1000–1350 nm), NIR-III (1600–1870 nm), and NIR-IV (2100–2300 nm).
source: NIR light can be divided into four distinct regions according to wavelength: NIR-I (700–950 nm), NIR-II (1000–1350 nm), NIR-III (1600–1870 nm), and NIR-IV (2100–2300 nm) (Sordillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This classification is supported by citation to Sordillo et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: NIR-III lasers possess relatively high penetration depths and low optical scattering effects compared with NIR-I and NIR-II lasers.
source: Compared with NIR-I and NIR-II lasers, NIR-III lasers possess relatively high penetration depths and low optical scattering effects (Horton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horton et al., 2013.

claim: The total attenuation lengths of human prostate and breast cancer are higher in the NIR-III optical windows than in other NIR regions.
source: The total attenuation lengths of human prostate and breast cancer have been revealed to be higher in the NIR-III optical windows than in the other NIR regions, confirming the potential for application of NIR-III lasers in tumor therapy (Choi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2016.

claim: The majority of MPNSTs are located on the body surface including head, neck, and extremity.
source: The majority of MPNSTs are located on the body surface including head, neck, and extremity (Le Guellec et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Le Guellec et al., 2016.

claim: NIR-III treatment involves a better wavelength range for tissue containing high collagen than conventional NIR-I treatment.
source: Sordillo et al., 2017 previously demonstrated that NIR-III treatment appears to involve a better wavelength range for tissue containing high collagen than conventional NIR-I treatment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sordillo et al., 2017.

claim: Collagen expression is significantly upregulated in MPNSTs.
source: In addition, a previous genetic profiling study has revealed that collagen expression is significantly upregulated in MPNSTs (Karube et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Karube et al., 2006.

claim: The safety of NIR-III has been widely demonstrated in various medical applications, including optical imaging, eye disease treatment, and cosmetic treatments.
source: Moreover, the safety of NIR-III has been widely demonstrated in various medical applications, including optical imaging (Shi et al., 2016b), eye disease treatment (Sakimoto et al., 2006), and even cosmetic treatments (Adatto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2016b; Sakimoto et al., 2006; and Adatto et al., 2017.

claim: The temperature of an aqueous solution increased gradually with increasing irradiation time and power density of the NIR-III laser.
source: The temperature of the aqueous solution increased gradually with increasing irradiation time and power density (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The 1.5 W cm–2 NIR-III laser caused an ~40°C temperature increase within 10 min in aqueous solution.
source: Notably, the 1.5 W cm–2 laser caused an ~40°C temperature increase within 10 min.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of temperature changes.

claim: The temperature of chicken breast surface rapidly increased from 27.2°C to 76.7°C within 10 min under NIR-III laser irradiation (1.5 W cm–2).
source: The temperature of the chicken breast surface rapidly increased from 27.2°C to 76.7°C within 10 min under NIR-III laser irradiation (1.5 W cm–2).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements in chicken breast tissue models.

claim: The difference between the temperature at 0 s and the temperature at 600 s (ΔT) was still over 10°C even when a chicken breast of 10 mm thickness was used to block the radiation.
source: The difference between the temperature at 0 s and the temperature at 600 s (ΔT) was still over 10°C even when a chicken breast of 10 mm thickness was used to block the radiation.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of tissue penetration.

claim: In the 5 min group, the 0.25 W cm–2 NIR-III laser induced a 25% reduction in STS26T cell viability.
source: In the 5 min group, the 0.25 W cm–2 NIR-III laser induced a 25% reduction in cell viability, while lasers with higher power density all exhibited a strong killing effect.
evidence: This is based on CCK-8 cell viability assay data.

claim: In the 10 min group, NIR-III irradiation caused maximum cell death regardless of the power density in STS26T cells.
source: In the 10 min group, NIR-III irradiation caused maximum cell death regardless of the power density.
evidence: This is based on CCK-8 cell viability assay data.

claim: The NIR-III laser (1 W cm–2) demonstrated almost 100% cell killing efficiency after penetrating chicken skin thickness of 4 mm in STS26T cells.
source: The NIR-III laser (1 W cm–2) demonstrated almost 100% cell killing efficiency after penetrating chicken skin thickness of 4 mm (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: For the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 2 min), NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min), NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 10 min), NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min), and NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 10 min) groups, the late apoptotic and dead cell populations reached almost 100%.
source: For the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 2 min), NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min), NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 10 min), NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min), and NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 10 min) groups, the late apoptotic and dead cell populations reached almost 100%, confirming the outstanding photothermal ablation effect of the NIR-III laser (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometric analysis data shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: In the STS26T xenograft model, the tumor temperature increased from 32.9°C and 33.9°C to 60.2°C and 75.4°C within 10 min of irradiation at the low (ΔT=27.3°C) and high (ΔT=41.5°C) power densities, respectively.
source: In the STS26T xenograft model (Figure 5a and b), the tumor temperature increased from 32.9°C and 33.9°C to 60.2°C and 75.4°C within 10 min of irradiation at the low (ΔT=27.3°C) and high (ΔT=41.5°C) power densities, respectively.
evidence: This is based on in vivo temperature measurements shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Effective photothermal ablation of subcutaneous xenograft tumors could be achieved at a depth of 4.5 mm in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 10 min) group.
source: It was revealed that effective photothermal ablation of subcutaneous xenograft tumors could be achieved at a depth of 4.5 mm in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 10 min) group.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of tumor sections at different depths.

claim: In the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 10 min) group, the effective photothermal ablation depth was over 7.5 mm.
source: However, in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 10 min) group, the effective photothermal ablation depth was over 7.5 mm, as revealed by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, Ki-67 immunohistochemical staining, and Cleaved-Caspase 3 immunohistochemical staining (Figure 5f–h) and the corresponding statistic analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 5f-h and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four out of seven mice in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group had tumor recurrence after 15 days.
source: However, four out of seven mice in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group had tumor recurrence after 15 days.
evidence: This is based on long-term observation of tumor-bearing mice.

claim: The tumors in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group were completely eradicated.
source: In comparison, the tumors in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group were completely eradicated (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is based on long-term observation data shown in Figure 6b and c.

claim: No significant pathological toxicity was observed in major organs in the two groups treated with PTT.
source: No significant pathological toxicity was observed in the two groups treated with PTT, and all of the mice demonstrated negligible weight fluctuations (Figure 6f), confirming that NIR-III-induced photothermal ablation had negligible adverse effects.
evidence: This is based on H&E staining of major organs and body weight measurements shown in Figure 6f and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) pathway (hsa04141) was among the most enriched pathways in STS26T tumors after NIR-III treatment.
source: According to Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses, the protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) pathway (hsa04141) were among the most enriched pathways (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is based on KEGG enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: NIR-III treatment could lead to ER stress in STS26T xenograft tumors.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the genes related to the protein processing in ER pathway (hsa04141) was further performed, which revealed that the key biological processes including the ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process, the response to unfold protein were enriched, indicating that NIR-III treatment could lead to ER stress in STS26T xenograft tumors (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: ATF4 and ATF6B were among the top upregulated mRNAs related to protein processing in ER pathway in STS26T tumors after NIR-III treatment.
source: It could be found that the key transcription factors regulating the UPR (ATF4 and ATF6B) were among the top upregulated mRNAs related to protein processing in ER pathway (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis confirmed the significant upregulation of ATF4 and ATF6B in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group.
source: RT-qPCR analysis also confirmed the significant upregulation of ATF4 and ATF6B in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: P4HB and HSPA1A were the most significantly upregulated ER chaperone genes in STS26T tumors after NIR-III treatment.
source: We identified the most significantly upregulated ER chaperones genes P4HB and HSP1A1 and further confirmed the upregulation of these two genes using RT-qPCR (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway (hsa04120) was enriched in STS26T tumors after NIR-III treatment.
source: According to KEGG enrichment analyses, the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway (hsa04120) was also enriched (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is based on KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The ER pathway was not enriched in S462 cells after NIR-III treatment.
source: However, the ER pathway was not enriched in the analyses, indicating that heterogeneity exists in response to NIR-III laser treatment among different MPNST cell types.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of S462 tumors.

claim: STS26T cells exhibited stronger resistance to NIR-III laser treatment than S462 cells.
source: Notably, STS26T cells exhibited stronger resistance to NIR-III laser treatment than S462 cells, as demonstrated by flow cytometric analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometric analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ER stress response (ERSR) enabled a proportion of STS26T cells to survive the NIR-III laser treatment through improving protein-folding capacity and ubiquitylating unfolded proteins.
source: Therefore, it can be speculated that the ER stress response (ERSR) enabled a proportion of STS26T cells to survive the NIR-III laser treatment through improving protein-folding capacity and ubiquitylating unfolded proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the RNA-seq and pathway analysis results.

claim: The combination of NIR-III laser treatment with an ER stress inhibitor (such as icariin or ghrelin) could potentially increase therapeutic effectiveness.
source: In addition, it is speculated that the combination of NIR-III laser treatment with an ER stress inhibitor (such as icariin or ghrelin) could potentially increase therapeutic effectiveness (Wang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019), which should be further verified in future studies.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Wang et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: The power safety limit for the NIR-III laser is higher than that for NIR-I and NIR-II lasers.
source: In addition, the power safety limit for the NIR-III laser is higher than that for NIR-I and NIR-II lasers, which in turn leads to efficient and safe tumor ablation (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1c-d.

claim: The photothermal conversion of the NIR-III laser is attributed to the thermal molecular movement of the irradiated object after laser irradiation.
source: In principle, the photothermal conversion of the NIR-III laser is attributed to the thermal molecular movement of the irradiated object after laser irradiation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on physical principles.

claim: The relatively high collagen content of MPNSTs ensures the efficiency of photothermal tumor ablation with the NIR-III laser.
source: The relatively high collagen content of MPNSTs ensure the efficiency of photothermal tumor ablation and make the NIR-III laser a suitable and potent therapeutic modality that has potential for use in clinical applications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of collagen expression in MPNSTs and NIR-III properties.

claim: The photothermal effects of NIR-III could be more concentrated in MPNSTs than in adjacent normal skin and soft tissue.
source: Therefore, the photothermal effects of NIR-III could be more concentrated in MPNSTs than in adjacent normal skin and soft tissue.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the high collagen content in MPNSTs and NIR-III properties.

claim: NIR-III laser would effectively induce photothermal ablation of MPNSTs due to their surface layout characteristics.
source: Therefore, it could be boldly speculated that NIR-III laser would effectively induce photothermal ablation of MPNSTs due to their surface layout characteristics.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the surface location of MPNSTs and NIR-III penetration properties.

claim: Two MPNST cell lines (STS26T and S462) were used for in vitro experiments.
source: Two representative MPNST cell lines, STS26T and S462, were utilized for in vitro experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: S462 was derived from an NF1-MPNST patient, whereas STS26T was derived from a sporadic MPNST patient.
source: S462 was derived from an NF1-MPNST patient, whereas STS26T was derived from a sporadic MPNST patient.
evidence: This is a description of the cell line origins.

claim: The 1650 nm NIR-III laser used in this work was composed of laser diodes, a collimator lens, a photodetector, a spectroscope, focusing lenses, and an optical fiber interface.
source: The 1650 nm NIR-III laser used in this work was composed of laser diodes, a collimator lens, a photodetector, a spectroscope, focusing lenses, and an optical fiber interface (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a description of the laser system shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Adjustment of the laser power had a negligible effect on the change in aqueous solution temperature for the NIR-I (808 nm) laser.
source: For the NIR-I group, adjustment of the laser power had a negligible effect on the change in aqueous solution temperature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the NIR-II group, an increase in power density elevated the aqueous solution temperature to a certain extent, but the maximum temperature difference was controlled within 15°C regardless of the duration.
source: In contrast, in the NIR-II group, an increase in power density elevated the aqueous solution temperature to a certain extent. However, the maximum temperature difference was controlled within 15°C regardless of the duration (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The temperature range varied from 36.6–91.1°C with laser power and fat thickness in pig fat penetration experiments.
source: Notably, temperature range (36.6–91.1°C) varied with laser power and fat thickness.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements in pig fat models.

claim: Similar attenuation of photothermal efficiency could be obtained regardless of whether the biological tissue was chicken breast or pig fat.
source: In addition, the temperature alterations at various tissue depths indicated that similar attenuation of photothermal efficiency could be obtained regardless of whether the biological tissue was chicken breast or pig fat (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of tissue penetration data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: A significant increase in S462 cell viability was observed with a chicken skin thickness of 6 mm.
source: Similar results were obtained in the S462 cell groups (Figure 4c and d). A significant increase in S462 cell viability was observed with a chicken skin thickness of 6 mm.
evidence: This is based on cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Significant cell death occurred in NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group, the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 2 min) group, and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) groups in both STS26T and S462 cells.
source: The results demonstrated that significant cell death occurred in NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group, the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 2 min) group, and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) groups in both STS26T and S462 cells (Figure 4e and f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on calcein-AM/PI assay data shown in Figure 4e, f, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After adjustment of the laser power density and irradiation time, similar increasing trends were observed in the S462 xenograft group for the low (ΔT=18.6°C) and high (ΔT=30.7°C) power densities.
source: Additionally, after adjustment of the laser power density and irradiation time, similar increasing trends were observed in the S462 xenograft group for the low (ΔT=18.6°C) and high (ΔT=30.7°C) power densities (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is based on in vivo temperature measurements shown in Figure 5c and d.

claim: More necrotic regions were observed in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group than in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group.
source: More necrotic regions were observed in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group than in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group.
evidence: This is based on H&E staining analysis of tumor sections.

claim: Apoptosis occurred in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group according to TUNEL assays, but the apoptosis in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group was more obvious.
source: In addition, apoptosis occurred in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group according to TUNEL assays, but the apoptosis in the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group was more obvious (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: All of the mice demonstrated negligible weight fluctuations after NIR-III treatment.
source: No significant pathological toxicity was observed in the two groups treated with PTT, and all of the mice demonstrated negligible weight fluctuations (Figure 6f), confirming that NIR-III-induced photothermal ablation had negligible adverse effects.
evidence: This is based on body weight measurements shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Significant transcriptional alterations were observed in STS26T tumors after NIR-III treatment.
source: In STS26T tumors, significant transcriptional alterations were observed and were further analyzed (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Both upregulated and downregulated overlapping mRNAs were found in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group compared with control group in STS26T tumors.
source: Both upregulated and downregulated overlapping mRNAs were found in the NIR-III (0.5 W cm–2, 5 min) group and the NIR-III (1 W cm–2, 5 min) group compared with control group (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claim: ATF4 and ATF6 contribute to stress relief and survival by inducing the expression of ER chaperones.
source: It was demonstrated in previous studies that ATF4 and ATF6B contributed to stress relief and survival by inducing the expression of ER chaperones, which have critical functions in facilitating protein folding and assembly.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The UPR regulated by ATF4 and ATF6 upregulates the components of ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
source: In addition to ER chaperones, the UPR regulated by ATF4 and ATF6 also upregulates the components of ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about UPR mechanisms.

claim: Proteins that do not properly fold within a certain time are targeted for ERAD, which efficiently retro-translocates them from the ER into the cytosol for degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Proteins that do not properly fold within a certain time are targeted for ERAD, which efficiently retro-translocates them from the ER into the cytosol for degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ERAD mechanisms.

claim: Heterogeneity exists in response to NIR-III laser treatment among different MPNST cell types.
source: However, the ER pathway was not enriched in the analyses, indicating that heterogeneity exists in response to NIR-III laser treatment among different MPNST cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different RNA-seq results between STS26T and S462 cells.

claim: ER stress is a condition during which a variety of pathological conditions including high temperature may impede the capacity of cells to properly fold secretory and transmembrane proteins in the ER and lead to the accumulation of misfolded proteins.
source: ER stress is a condition during which a variety of pathological conditions including high temperature may impede the capacity of cells to properly fold secretory and transmembrane proteins in the ER and lead to the accumulation of misfolded proteins.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ER stress mechanisms, supported by citation to Qi and Chen, 2019.

claim: Cells with ER stress can initiate a self-protection mechanism termed the unfolded protein response (UPR) that induces a set of transcriptional and translational events to restore ER homeostasis.
source: Cells with ER stress can initiate a self-protection mechanism termed the unfolded protein response (UPR) that induces a set of transcriptional and translational events to restore ER homeostasis (Qi and Chen, 2019).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about UPR mechanisms, supported by citation to Qi and Chen, 2019.

claim: The most significantly upregulated mRNAs in the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis pathway include UBA3, UBE2E1, and HERC3.
source: The most significantly upregulated mRNAs including UBA3, UBE2E1, and HERC3 were listed in Supplementary file 3.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: It is applicable to combine preoperative NIR-III photothermal laser treatment and surgery to reduce the scope and the risk of surgery for MPNSTs.
source: Therefore, it is applicable to combine preoperative NIR-III photothermal laser treatment and surgery to reduce the scope and the risk of surgery.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: The postoperative application of NIR-III laser treatment at the resection margin could be a potent modality to reduce the risk of local recurrence.
source: The postoperative application of NIR-III laser treatment at the resection margin could be a potent modality to reduce the risk of local recurrence.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: STS26T MPNST cells strongly enhanced the protein processing capacity of the ER to survive the ER stress induced by NIR-III laser treatment.
source: Mechanically, it is possible that STS26T MPNST cells strongly enhanced the protein processing capacity of the ER to survive the ER stress induced by NIR-III laser treatment.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the RNA-seq and pathway analysis results.

claim: An optimal effect can be achieved by optimizing the power density and irradiation time of the NIR-III laser despite individual differences in molecular response and treatment efficiency.
source: Although the tumor ablation effect is influenced by individual differences in molecular response and treatment efficiency, an optimal effect can still be achieved by optimizing the power density and irradiation time of the NIR-III laser.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing different responses between cell lines.

claim: The NIR-III photothermal treatment efficiency varied among individuals, which was possibly influenced by different endoplasmic reticulum stress responses.
source: We found that although the NIR-III photothermal treatment efficiency varied among individuals, which was possibly influenced by different endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, the expected antineoplastic effect was ultimately achieved after adjustment of the power density and radiation duration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The expected antineoplastic effect was ultimately achieved after adjustment of the power density and radiation duration.
source: We found that although the NIR-III photothermal treatment efficiency varied among individuals, which was possibly influenced by different endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, the expected antineoplastic effect was ultimately achieved after adjustment of the power density and radiation duration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo experimental results.

claim: This PTAs-free PTT strategy possesses unique advantages for the development of clinical application and the improvement of patient prognosis due to the excellent biocompatibility and predominant photothermal conversion efficiency of NIR-III laser.
source: This PTAs-free PTT strategy possesses unique advantages for the development of clinical application and the improvement of patient prognosis due to the excellent biocompatibility and predominant photothermal conversion efficiency of NIR-III laser.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall experimental results.

claim: This PTAs-free NIR-III PTT approach may be further generalized for the treatment of other benign and malignant skin and soft-tissue tumors.
source: It is expected that this PTAs-free NIR-III PTT approach may be further generalized for the treatment of other benign and malignant skin and soft-tissue tumors.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential broader applications.
